[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-CAP-DESC-0.2.03.md#perimeter-defense]

## Perimeter Defense

**Parent L1**: Network Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Perimeter Defense governs the inspection and filtering of north-south traffic at the boundaries between enterprise network segments and external networks, including the internet, partner networks, and client tenant connections. It establishes stateful traffic inspection, ingress and egress policy enforcement, and threat-aware screening at network edges. The capability ensures that only authorized traffic patterns traverse network boundaries and that anomalous or malicious traffic is detected and blocked before reaching interior network segments.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.AC — Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control; PR.DS — Data Security for traffic in transit); directly addresses the requirement to govern what enters and exits enterprise network boundaries
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Perimeter Defense evolves under Zero Trust from a single hard perimeter to a set of graduated enforcement points at each network segment boundary; the capability is retained in a Zero Trust architecture but its scope narrows — it provides the outermost inspection layer rather than the sole trust boundary
**Key Stakeholders**: Network engineering, security architecture, infrastructure platform teams, security operations center
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-FIREWALL-2.2.01](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-FIREWALL-2.2.01.md)
**Capability Boundary**: This capability governs layer-3 and layer-4 traffic filtering at network boundaries; application-layer HTTP/S traffic filtering is the Application Traffic Filtering capability; traffic inspection within network segments is the Network Segmentation capability

## Application Traffic Filtering

**Parent L1**: Network Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: Application Traffic Filtering provides layer-7 inspection of HTTP/S traffic, API calls, and web application requests to detect and block application-layer attacks before they reach backend services. It encompasses Web Application Firewall (WAF) capabilities for protecting web-facing applications and API gateway security controls for governing API traffic flows. The capability inspects request content, detects attack patterns (including OWASP Top 10 web and API attack patterns), enforces traffic rate limits, and applies protocol-level validation rules. It operates as the network-layer enforcement complement to application-layer input validation.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.DS); application-layer attacks targeting web and API surfaces represent the highest-volume category of external threats to enterprise services
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Application Traffic Filtering is a network-layer Zero Trust enforcement point for application access; it enforces that only well-formed, policy-compliant requests reach application services — no traffic that bypasses this layer should be treated as implicitly trusted
**Key Stakeholders**: Security architects, application platform teams, API platform owners, DevSecOps teams
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-WAF-2.2.02](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-WAF-2.2.02.md), [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-API-GW-2.2.04.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Application Traffic Filtering inspects traffic at the network entry point for applications; application-internal input validation and business logic security are Application Security domain responsibilities; TLS decryption to enable plaintext inspection is the Traffic Inspection capability

## Traffic Inspection and Encryption Enforcement

**Parent L1**: Network Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Traffic Inspection and Encryption Enforcement provides a governed capability to inspect TLS-encrypted traffic at designated inspection points by performing TLS termination, security analysis of the decrypted payload, and re-encryption before forwarding to the destination. It also enforces minimum encryption standards — prohibiting deprecated protocol versions and cipher suites — across network paths where encryption is required. This capability addresses the architectural problem that encrypted traffic, while essential for confidentiality, creates blind spots in network security monitoring that threat actors exploit to exfiltrate data and communicate with compromised systems without detection.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.DS — Data Security) and CSF Detect (DE.AE — Adverse Event Analysis); encrypted traffic inspection restores the visibility that security monitoring requires without eliminating encryption as a control
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Zero Trust requires that all traffic — including encrypted traffic — be subject to policy evaluation; this capability enables security policy enforcement on encrypted flows by providing authorized inspection points, consistent with the Zero Trust principle that no traffic should be exempt from monitoring
**Key Stakeholders**: Security architects, network engineering, security operations center, compliance teams
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-TLS-INSP-2.2.06](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-TLS-INSP-2.2.06.md)
**Capability Boundary**: This capability governs inspection of encrypted traffic at designated network points; certificate lifecycle management and PKI governance are Identity Security domain responsibilities; application-layer encryption (e.g., field-level encryption, database encryption) is outside the scope of this network capability

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-CAP-DESC-0.2.03.md#network-segmentation-and-microsegmentation]

## Network Segmentation and Microsegmentation

**Parent L1**: Network Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Network Segmentation and Microsegmentation establishes the subdivision of the enterprise network fabric — including cloud VPCs, data center VLANs, and container network overlays — into discrete segments governed by explicit, allow-list access controls. Microsegmentation extends traditional VLAN-based segmentation to workload-level granularity, enabling individual services or containers to have independently governed network communication policies. The capability directly limits lateral movement: a compromised workload can only communicate with the systems that its policy explicitly permits, regardless of network proximity.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.AC — Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control); microsegmentation is the primary architectural control for limiting lateral movement following an initial compromise
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Network segmentation is a direct architectural implementation of the Zero Trust principle "assume breach, minimize blast radius" — by removing implicit east-west trust between workloads, the impact of a compromised host is bounded by its explicit policy permit-list rather than by the network segment it happens to occupy
**Key Stakeholders**: Infrastructure and platform engineering, cloud architecture teams, security architects, application development teams
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-MICROSEG-2.2.03](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-MICROSEG-2.2.03.md); [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-MICROPERIMETER-2.2.13](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-MICROPERIMETER-2.2.13.md)
**Capability Boundary**: This capability governs network-layer communication policies between workloads; identity-based access control for application resources is the Identity Security capability; host-based process isolation is the Endpoint Security capability

## Zero Trust Network Access

**Parent L1**: Network Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Zero Trust Network Access (ZTNA) is the capability that provides workforce and partner access to enterprise applications and services through a software-defined access broker that evaluates identity, device posture, and contextual signals before establishing per-session, scoped network access. It replaces or augments VPN-centric remote access models that grant broad network access upon authentication with a model in which access is granted per application, per session, with no lateral network visibility. ZTNA is the primary architectural mechanism through which the Zero Trust principle "never trust the network, always verify the identity" is operationalized for remote and hybrid access patterns.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.AC); ZTNA directly addresses the security limitations of traditional VPN access — broad network exposure, static session lifecycles, and limited device posture enforcement
**Zero Trust Relevance**: ZTNA is the most direct network-layer realization of Zero Trust Architecture per NIST SP 800-207; it implements the Software Defined Perimeter pattern in which network access is dynamically scoped to the minimum required for each authenticated, authorized, device-posture-verified session
**Key Stakeholders**: Remote workforce users, IT operations, security architects, endpoint management teams
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-ZTNA-2.2.07](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-ZTNA-2.2.07.md)
**Capability Boundary**: ZTNA governs network access for remote and hybrid access patterns; identity verification and device posture assessment are provided as inputs by the Identity Security and Endpoint Security capabilities; access policy for specific applications is an Application Security responsibility consumed through ZTNA's policy evaluation

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-CAP-DESC-0.2.03.md#dns-security]

## DNS Security

**Parent L1**: Network Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: DNS Security protects the DNS resolution layer from abuse as an attack vector and provides threat detection visibility through DNS traffic analytics. It encompasses DNS-based threat intelligence filtering (blocking resolution of known malicious domains), DNS over HTTPS/TLS enforcement, split-horizon DNS governance, and DNS query logging for security analytics. DNS is a uniquely high-value threat vector because it is universally permitted through firewalls, operates at high volume, and is used by attackers for command-and-control communication, data exfiltration via DNS tunneling, and malware domain resolution. DNS Security addresses this threat surface architecturally.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.AC) and CSF Detect (DE.AE); DNS-layer controls provide a detection signal with extremely high coverage because nearly all network communication involves DNS resolution
**Zero Trust Relevance**: DNS resolution is the first step in most network communication; a governed DNS layer provides an early enforcement and monitoring point that operates independently of application-layer controls — aligning with Zero Trust's principle of defense in depth across multiple independent control layers
**Key Stakeholders**: Network engineering, security operations center, platform engineering, security architects
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-DNS-SEC-2.2.08](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-DNS-SEC-2.2.08.md)
**Capability Boundary**: DNS Security governs DNS resolution as a security control layer; DNS service configuration and resolution infrastructure are network operations responsibilities; domain registration and public DNS management are IT operations responsibilities outside the scope of this capability

## DDoS Protection

**Parent L1**: Network Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase A–B
**Description**: DDoS Protection detects and mitigates distributed denial-of-service attacks targeting enterprise internet-facing services and platform infrastructure. It spans volumetric attack mitigation (absorbing or diverting high-bandwidth traffic floods), protocol attack mitigation (SYN floods, reflection/amplification attacks), and application-layer attack mitigation (HTTP floods, Slowloris, API-targeted attacks). The capability operates in layers — network-edge mitigation for volumetric attacks, transit provider absorption for the largest attacks, and application-proximate mitigation for sophisticated layer-7 attacks. DDoS availability risk is particularly significant for healthcare government services where unplanned outages directly affect benefit delivery.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.DS — Data Security) and CSF Respond (RS.MI — Incident Mitigation); availability of healthcare program services is a regulatory obligation — unmitigated DDoS events can constitute reportable security incidents under certain contractual frameworks
**Zero Trust Relevance**: DDoS Protection is not a Zero Trust control but a resilience capability; it ensures the availability of the enforcement points (perimeter firewalls, WAF, API gateways, ZTNA brokers) on which Zero Trust network controls depend — if enforcement points are unavailable, the control plane fails
**Key Stakeholders**: Platform engineering, network engineering, security architecture, service delivery leadership, security operations center
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-DDOS-2.2.09](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-DDOS-2.2.09.md)
**Capability Boundary**: DDoS Protection governs availability controls for network-accessible services; application availability and redundancy architecture is the Application Security domain; incident response following a DDoS event is the Security Operations capability

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-CAP-DESC-0.2.03.md#network-monitoring-and-visibility]

## Network Monitoring and Visibility

**Parent L1**: Network Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Network Monitoring and Visibility provides continuous capture, analysis, and correlation of network traffic metadata, flow records, and packet-level data to establish behavioral baselines, detect anomalous communication patterns, and support network forensic investigation. It encompasses NetFlow/IPFIX collection, network detection and response (NDR), east-west traffic visibility in cloud and container environments, and integration of network telemetry with the enterprise SIEM. Network monitoring provides a detection layer that is independent of endpoint and application instrumentation — enabling detection of threats that evade host-based controls by exploiting the network layer.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Detect (DE.AE — Adverse Event Analysis; DE.CM — Continuous Monitoring); network visibility is a primary input to security operations detection workflows and a prerequisite for effective network forensics during incident investigation
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Zero Trust requires continuous verification — not just at the moment of access; network monitoring provides the runtime behavioral signal that enables continuous assessment of whether observed traffic patterns are consistent with authorized access grants, triggering investigation or revocation when anomalies are detected
**Key Stakeholders**: Security operations center, threat detection teams, incident response teams, network engineering, compliance and audit
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-NETMON-2.2.10](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-NETMON-2.2.10.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Network monitoring captures and analyzes traffic at the network layer; security incident investigation and response are Security Operations capabilities that consume network monitoring output; endpoint behavioral analytics are Endpoint Security capabilities

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-CAP-DESC-0.2.03.md#cloud-network-security]

## Cloud Network Security

**Parent L1**: Network Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Cloud Network Security governs the architecture and operational governance of cloud-native network constructs — including VPC/VNet design, security groups, network access control lists (NACLs), transit gateways, private service endpoints, VPC peering, and service mesh configurations — to enforce segmentation, access control, and traffic inspection in cloud environments. The capability addresses the specific challenges of cloud network governance: infrastructure-as-code-defined network topology that can change at high velocity, cloud-native network controls that have no direct equivalent in traditional data center architecture, and multi-account or multi-subscription environments where network governance must be consistently enforced through policy-as-code.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.AC, PR.DS); cloud network security is a foundational prerequisite for safe cloud adoption — without architectural governance of cloud network topology, cloud environments produce ungoverned segmentation and access control postures
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Cloud-native environments lack a physical perimeter by design; Cloud Network Security applies Zero Trust network principles to cloud architecture — every VPC boundary, security group rule, and service endpoint represents an explicit policy decision rather than an implicit trust grant based on co-tenancy in the same cloud account
**Key Stakeholders**: Cloud architecture teams, platform engineering, security architects, DevSecOps teams, infrastructure-as-code owners
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-CLOUD-NET-2.2.11](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-CLOUD-NET-2.2.11.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Cloud Network Security governs cloud-native network architecture; cloud identity and access management is the Identity Security capability; container and workload security beyond network controls is the Endpoint Security capability; data protection controls within cloud storage and databases are the Data Security capability

[strategy/guidance/security/Network/GUID-SEC-NETWORK-CAP-DESC-0.2.03.md#traffic-control-and-policy-enforcement]

## Traffic Control and Policy Enforcement

**Parent L1**: Network Security
**ADM Phase**: Phase B
**Description**: Traffic Control and Policy Enforcement governs routing policy, protocol enforcement, and traffic shaping across enterprise network paths, ensuring traffic flows conform to architectural intent and that protocol deviations and unauthorized traffic patterns are detected and blocked. It encompasses BGP route policy governance, protocol allowlisting and blocking, egress traffic filtering for data exfiltration prevention at the network layer, and enforcement of traffic flow policies between network segments. The capability ensures that the network fabric behaves according to its designed architecture — both in normal operation and when adversarial actors attempt to manipulate routing or exploit permissive protocol policies.
**Strategic Alignment**: CSF Protect (PR.AC, PR.DS); protocol enforcement and egress filtering are network-layer controls that complement identity and application-layer controls in a defense-in-depth strategy
**Zero Trust Relevance**: Traffic control enforces that network traffic follows authorized paths and uses authorized protocols; it closes exfiltration and lateral movement paths that might bypass higher-level identity and application controls — a necessary complement to identity-centric Zero Trust enforcement
**Key Stakeholders**: Network engineering, security architects, cloud platform teams, security operations center
**Related ABBs**: [GUID-SEC-NETWORK-TRAFFIC-CTRL-2.2.12](GUID-SEC-NETWORK-TRAFFIC-CTRL-2.2.12.md)
**Capability Boundary**: Traffic Control governs protocol and routing policy enforcement; application-layer traffic filtering is the Application Traffic Filtering capability; firewall stateful inspection at boundaries is the Perimeter Defense capability
